summary: John C. Frain re-examines the long-run correlation between average money growth and average inflation using a multi-country IMF International Financial Statistics data set of 88-89 countries with at least 25 years of data. He finds strong correlations that persist when high-inflation countries are excluded, contradicting De Grauwe and Polan (2001), and finds the response for low-inflation countries is less than one-to-one under OLS but not inconsistent with a unit response under a variable coefficient model. The paper argues the results support the European Central Bank's monetary analysis pillar, while stressing the findings are long-run and imply no direction of causality.
one_line: Frain's 2004 paper finds a strong long-run link between money growth and inflation across countries, challenging De Grauwe and Polan and supporting ECB monetary analysis.
key_facts: The paper was published in The Economic and Social Review, Vol. 35, No. 3, Winter 2004, pp. 251-266.
The author, John C. Frain, is affiliated with the Central Bank and Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ireland and Trinity College Dublin.
McCandless and Weber (1995) examined data covering a 30-year period for 110 countries using three definitions of money (M0, M1 and M2).
De Grauwe and Polan (2001) concluded that the correlation between inflation and money growth is entirely due to high inflation countries in their sample.
The data used are from the January 2003 International Financial Statistics CD-ROM of the International Monetary Fund.
The analysis limited the sample to countries with at least 25 years of annual data, yielding 89, 88 and 87 countries for M0, M1 and M2 respectively.
For the full sample, the coefficient on the monetary growth variables is close to one (minimum .938, maximum 1.074).
For lower inflation countries (less than 10 per cent average inflation), the coefficients on monetary growth remain significant but all are significantly less than one.
The excess money growth variable is defined as money growth minus real output growth plus price growth, i.e. ∆m̂i = ∆mi – ∆y + ∆p.
A minimum sample size of 15 is used in the recursive estimates, which corresponds to an inflation rate of about 4 per cent.
The variable coefficient model is estimated with Kalman filter techniques, assuming a diffuse initialisation of the filter.
For the excess M1 full sample regression, the coefficient is 1.012 with a standard error of 0.012 and R² of 0.99.
The ECB defines price stability as a year-on-year increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices for the euro area of below 2 per cent.
The paper states that its results are long run and say nothing about any short-run relationship between money growth and inflation.
De Grauwe and Polan's full sample M1 regression used 165 countries and reported a money growth coefficient of 2.1018.
